fields.h1: Build a Pricing Survey and Test Prices Before You Set Them
fields.hero_description: Build a pricing survey that asks what buyers would pay, lowers the price after a no, and saves each answer to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What Goes Into a Pricing Survey Build
fields.features_subheading: What Emergent builds behind the price questions, and where each answer goes once a respondent submits it.
fields.feature_1:
Price questions drafted from your product

Describe the product, who buys it, and the price you have in mind. Emergent drafts the survey and its logic, and you change any question later by typing a follow-up prompt.
fields.feature_2:
A lower price after every no

List your price steps, say $59, $49, and $39. The app shows the same buying question at the next step down to anyone who says no, and records the price each one accepts.
fields.feature_3:
One price question per screen

Respondents answer one price question at a time, with the product description kept above it. Nobody sees the next price until they have answered the one in front of them.
fields.feature_4:
Every answer saved with its price

Each answer is a row in a database you own: the respondent, the price shown, the answer, and the date. Sort it by price step or customer group as soon as the survey closes.
fields.feature_5:
No cap on responses

Send the survey to every customer on your list. Emergent sets no response cap, so a 50-person pilot and the full send to 2,000 customers run on the same survey and database.
fields.feature_6:
The full code in your GitHub

On paid plans, export the full code of the survey and its price logic to your GitHub repository, and keep it next to the rest of your own product code from that day on.

fields.usecase_heading: How Four Teams Tested a Price
fields.tab_content_1:
A $24 box from four price questions

Cobbleway Coffee asked 312 subscribers four price questions before launching a tasting box. The median answers came back at $14 for too cheap, $19 for a bargain, $26 for getting expensive, and $32 for too expensive. Cobbleway set the launch price at $24, under the $26 point where the box starts to feel expensive.
fields.tab_content_2:
A no at $59 brings the question back at $49

Sketchwell put one question to 200 trial users: how likely are you to buy at $59 a month? Anyone who picked a not likely answer at $59 saw the question again at $49, then at $39. At $49, 102 users would buy, or $4,998 a month, more than either other price brings in. Sketchwell priced the plan at $49.
fields.tab_content_3:
19 customers who would cancel get a call

Bramblecote Pest Control is raising its quarterly plan to $135. The survey told 214 customers the new price and asked whether they would stay. Each of the 19 who said they would cancel went to Dana, the office manager, as a direct message in Slack, and she called them before the new price started.
fields.tab_content_4:
Team at $35 is the pick for 141 of 275

Tallyroom showed 275 small business owners three plan cards and asked each to pick the one they would buy: Starter at $15, Team at $35, or Pro at $70. Team drew 141 picks, Starter 88, and Pro 46. Tallyroom made Team the default plan at signup.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Pricing Survey
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to create a pricing survey that finds the price your buyers accept, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick the method that fits your price
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Describe the product before any price
fields.howto_step_1_des: Pick the method by what you already know. Van Westendorp fits when you don't have a target price in mind yet. A price ladder fits when you have a few prices to choose between and want the one that brings in the most revenue.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Send the survey to people who could realistically buy: trial users, current subscribers, or buyers in your category. Leave out staff, friends, and anyone outside your market, since their answers say little about what a real buyer would pay.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Open with a short description of the product: what it does, what is included, and whether it is billed monthly or yearly. Ask about price only after that screen, so every respondent judges the same offer.
fields.howto_step_4_des: If you have a target price, offer closed price options and put the target in the middle of your options. If you have none, use open number fields for the four price questions and let the answers set the range.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Add the logic that lowers the price
fields.howto_step_5_des: For a price ladder, ask how likely the respondent is to buy at your highest price. Anyone who picks one of the bottom three answers sees the same question at the next price down, until they accept or the ladder ends.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Send the survey to five people before the full list. Check that each price shows where it should, that the lower price appears after a no, and that every answer lands in the database next to the price shown.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Read the answers by price and decide
fields.howto_step_7_des: Once the survey closes, line up the answers for each price and pick the one you will charge. Keep the survey as it is, and run it again before the next price change so you can compare the two sets of answers.

faq_plan.a: A pricing survey is a research method that asks your target market directly what they would pay for a product or service. Run one before a launch or a price change. The answers point to a range of prices buyers accept, or to one price to charge.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a pricing survey?
faq_plan.a: Describe the product, the people who buy it, and the prices you want to test in a prompt to Emergent's AI survey builder. It builds the survey, the logic that moves between prices, and the database the answers go into. Test it with five people, then send it to your full list.

faq_plan.q: How many pricing survey questions should I ask?
faq_plan.a: Ask as few as your method needs. The Van Westendorp method uses four questions, covering too cheap, a bargain, expensive but worth it, and too expensive. A price ladder needs one buying question, asked again at lower prices. Add two or three questions about the respondent, such as company size or current plan, to split the answers by group.

faq_plan.q: What does a price sensitivity survey tell you?
faq_plan.a: It tells you where buyers start to see a price as too cheap and where they see it as too expensive, and the method plots the answers to define your acceptable price range. Respondents need to know the product to answer well. If few people have heard of it, run a brand awareness survey first.

faq_plan.q: What should a pricing survey template include?
faq_plan.a: It should include a short product description, the price questions for one method, and a few questions about who is answering. A generic pricing survey template leaves you rewriting the product description and every price step. Emergent drafts the survey from a prompt about your own product, and the first draft already names your prices and plans.

faq_plan.q: Are open-ended or multiple choice answers better in a pricing survey?
faq_plan.a: Multiple choice works better when you have a target price: place that target near the middle of the range you offer. An open number field works better when you have no target yet: the answers set the range instead of your options. Keep one format per question, and every answer to it stays comparable.

faq_plan.q: How do I run a pricing survey for a price increase?
faq_plan.a: Tell customers the new price and the date it starts, then ask one question: will they stay, might they stay, or would they cancel. Keep it out of your customer satisfaction survey and give the price question an answer of its own. A survey built with Emergent has no response cap, and it can go to every customer on the plan.

faq_plan.q: How does a pricing survey find the price with the most revenue?
faq_plan.a: It asks how likely people are to buy at each of several prices. Multiply each price by the number who would buy at it, and the highest result is your revenue peak. This is the Gabor-Granger method, and it does not factor in competitor pricing. Check what rivals charge before you settle.

faq_plan.q: Can pricing surveys test several plans at once?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Show plan cards that each carry a price and ask which one the respondent would buy. A conjoint analysis survey goes further: it shows respondents combinations of product attributes, one of which is price, and asks them to choose. Limit how many combinations you show any one respondent.

faq_plan.q: Should a pricing survey go to customers or prospects?
faq_plan.a: Send it to both, as two separate surveys. Prospects tell you what to charge at launch, and current customers tell you how a change will land with people already paying. Run the customer version apart from your customer experience survey. With Emergent, both surveys write to a database you own, and each answer sits beside the price shown.

plan.angle: The top 10 are method explainers from research vendors and panels (Voxco, SurveyMonkey, Qualtrics, Attest, quantilope) that define Van Westendorp, Gabor-Granger and conjoint, then hand the build to their own research product. None shows a pricing survey running for a small team: the questions on screen, the logic that lowers a price after a no, and what happens to the answers. This page defines the method choices in the FAQ and how-to, then shows four pricing surveys built from a prompt: a coffee roaster's four price questions for a new box, a design app's price ladder, a pest control company asking customers about a price increase, and a bookkeeping app's plan choice. Siblings own satisfaction, experience and market research; this page owns price.
